stories.headline: Two songwriters used AI to reach number one in Korea.
stories.what: MEOMURU's rock ballad The Adult I Dreamed Of, by the songwriting duo Glorywave (Lee Yong-seok and Choi Sung-hyuk), is the first AI-assisted song to top Melon's Top 100, Korea's most watched chart. The pair wrote the lyrics and used Suno for the melody, arrangement and vocals, then refined them; on Wednesday 25 November it was still at number one, more than a week after it reached the top on 13 November, with no fandom or TV promotion behind it.
stories.why: Two working songwriters with no fandom behind them reached the top of the country's biggest chart by writing the words themselves and letting AI play the band.

source.label: The Korea Times, 'AI music tops local chart: What you need to know', 26 Nov 2026 (KST)

The Korea Times counted four nonhuman acts, including a HYBE-backed VTuber project, putting out debut or predebut music in the last full week of November.
stories.why: A production company now sits in the same release week as the big K-pop agencies with a group nobody had to train for years.

stories.headline: An AI scouting app got 26 overlooked footballers signed.
stories.what: Footbao, a Swiss app built in Brazil, lets young players upload videos of themselves, which its AI scores on 24 performance indicators before analysts pass the best to scouts. It now has 170,000 registered players and more than 80 partner clubs in six countries, including Santos and Corinthians, and on 25 November 2026 said players in Switzerland, Germany and Austria can register from January 2027. Its own site counts 750 players referred to clubs and 26 signed.
stories.why: Clubs are finding signings through an app that watches thousands of teenagers they would never have paid a scout to see.

stories.headline: A NASCAR team gave its race car an AI voice for guests.
stories.what: Trackhouse Racing built 88Bot, an AI agent that speaks as Connor Zilisch's No. 88 Chevrolet: guests download an app, ask the car questions about the race and get live updates from its racing data. The team can host up to 60 VIP guests on a race day in a pit box that fits about eight, and the system draws on roughly 25,000 telemetry messages a second. Sports Business Journal first reported it on 23 November 2026, and some fans pushed back online.
stories.why: A race team is using AI to make its most valuable seats, the ones it sells to sponsors, more worth paying for.

stories.headline: Odeon's cinema assistant answers 40% of questions, no jobs lost.
stories.what: Odeon Cinemas told diginomica on 27 November 2026 that its AI assistant Odi, built on Zendesk, resolves about 40% of guest queries, from showtimes to ticket problems, while human agents take the harder ones. The chain says it gets up to 10,000 queries a week, satisfaction has risen over 18 months, and it has kept its service teams.
stories.why: Cinemas run on thin margins, and Odeon is using AI to absorb the busy weeks without cutting the people who handle the hard cases.

helps.who: cinema operators and their guest service staff

source.label: diginomica, 'Projecting success on EX and CX at Odeon Cinemas', Stuart Lauchlan, 27 Nov 2026

stories.headline: Norway's biggest paper uses AI on 200 stories a day.
stories.what: In a piece published on 27 November 2026, Christoph Trattner of the University of Bergen reported that VG asks an AI model for a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 new articles a day, with a second model checking the first. At Bergens Tidende, AI writes short versions of reporters' stories; the development editor says about one in ten needs a fix, almost never for hallucinations, and the paper has never published a critical mistake this way.
stories.why: A newsroom shows AI saving reporters time without letting errors into print, because the person checking already knows the story.

source.label: Fortune, 'I have a front-row seat to Norway's cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment', by Christoph Trattner, 27 Nov 2026

stories.headline: Der Spiegel's model finds a third of readers about to leave.
stories.what: Der Spiegel's lead data scientist, Alexander Held, published how the German news magazine built a machine-learning score for subscriber churn, in a WAN-IFRA piece on 23 November 2026. The riskiest group it flags, close to 10,000 subscriptions, cancels at 28% against a base rate of about 4%, and that group holds about 36% of everyone who leaves.
stories.why: A news publisher can now see a cancellation coming and act before the reader goes, which is subscription money kept.

source.label: WAN-IFRA, 'Addressing subscriber churn at Der Spiegel, part one: building the score', Alexander Held, 23 Nov 2026

stories.headline: Nine plugged its newspapers into business AI tools.
stories.what: Australian publisher Nine announced on 25 November 2026 a pilot that lets licensed business subscribers connect its journalism from The Australian Financial Review, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, Brisbane Times and WAtoday to their own AI tools through the Model Context Protocol. It is testing with a group of business clients before a wider commercial rollout through 2027.
stories.why: A newspaper group found a way to sell its journalism to AI users without giving it away to the AI companies.

source.label: Nine for Brands, 'Nine Leads With First-of-Its-Kind Authenticated MCP Publishing AI Pilot in Australia', 25 Nov 2026

stories.what: Canva made its MCP server generally available on 24 November 2026, letting AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini make and edit Canva designs, images and video. Canva says nearly 500,000 people signed up through MCP since October, usage grew 93% in a month, and the yearly revenue it expects from MCP has more than tripled since September.
stories.why: A design company found hundreds of thousands of new users by letting other companies' chatbots do the clicking.

helps.who: Canva and designers who work through AI assistants

source.label: The Next Web, 'Canva opens its design tools to AI agents and outside developers', 24 Nov 2026

stories.what: Sujal Jaiswar's AI-made Desi Batman series, in which Batman brushes his teeth by railway tracks and rides a buffalo to a 1999 Bollywood song, drew more than 25 million views in two weeks and took his Instagram account to about 749,000 followers.
